title: High-throughput light-sheet 3D microscopy of whole rodent brain microstructure for integration with MRI
authors: Hanmer, J. M.; D'Antonio, F.; Assimopoulos, S.; Manzano-Patron, J.-P.; Wood, S. C.; Tachrount, M.; Shen, Q.; Craig, M.; Lai, C.; Hickman, G. J.; Radfar, E.; Chisholm, K. I.; Farr, T. D.; Jasanoff, A.; Hoerder-Suabedissen, A.; Molnar, Z.; Ligneul, C.; Tisca, C.; Jbabdi, S.; Howard, A. F. D.; Miller, K. L.; de Guzman, E.; Lerch, J. P.; Sotiropoulos, S. N.
abstract: Whole-brain cellular mapping is essential for understanding how differences in cellular architecture shape brain organisation and function. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides whole-brain coverage in humans and animal models but is only indirectly sensitive to cellular features. Integrating MRI with whole-brain microscopy is therefore critical for interpreting existing microstructural MRI measures and developing more specific ones. Here, we present a scalable cross-resolution framework integrating 3D light-sheet microscopy (LSM) of intact rodent brains with diffusion MRI (dMRI). By combining active tissue clearing and immunolabelling with accelerated LSM acquisitions, we achieve multiplexed whole-brain mapping of neuronal and glial populations on timescales comparable to conventional histology and 2D microscopy. This throughput enables LSM and MRI integration at scale, linking macroscopic MRI contrasts to spatially-matched microscopic cellular features within the same tissue. We apply this framework across eight genetically diverse mouse strains to develop predictive models of 3D microscopy-derived cellular features from dMRI contrasts. We demonstrate that data-driven combinations of state-of-the-art multi-shell dMRI measures predict neuronal and astrocytic features better than individual contrasts, across all animals. Our approach enables 3D microscopy to guide the development and interpretation of biologically-specific microstructural MRI measures, with the potential for translation to the living human brain.

title: Molecular Modulation of the SAM-I Riboswitch Drives Global Dynamical Shifts
authors: Nair, V.; Niknam Hamidabad, M.; Erol, D.; Mansbach, R.
abstract: A surge in antimicrobial resistance in recent years has made protein-targeting antibiotics less effective against key pathogens. It is possible to expand the range of therapeutic targets by using RNA-based therapies, but it remains necessary to improve the molecular-level understanding of interactions between RNA and known and potential binders. The SAM-I riboswitch, which controls the transcriptional termination of gene expression involved in sulfur metabolism in most bacteria, is an excellent ligand target. Thus, understanding its behavior with and without ligand complexes would be helpful for drug design. Here, we studied the interactions between the SAM-I riboswitch and its natural ligand, SAM, which controls riboswitch function, and compared those to its interactions with the similar small molecule SAH, which does not control riboswitch function, and to its interactions with a potential binder JS4, identified via virtual screening. From our simulations, we deepen understanding of small molecule interactions with the SAM-I riboswitch on both a local and a distal level. The results reveal how differently ligands (SAM, SAH and JS4) can bind to and potentially induce conformational changes in the riboswitch. Our findings offer valuable insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying riboswitch RNA-ligand interactions for the design of more effective RNA-targeting therapeutics.

title: Hybrid RY-mers increase aDNA alignment sensitivity
abstract: One of the key steps in ancient DNA data analysis is the accurate identification of endogenous short reads that originate from the ancient genome. Currently, this step is performed using general-purpose sequence aligners, such as BWA-aln, with parameter settings optimized for sensitivity. This approach results in increased runtime, even relative to standard DNA alignment workflows, and is not sufficient for aligning samples that are highly divergent from a reference database. We introduce hybrid RY-mers, a seed construct designed to incorporate aDNA-specific sequence damage. We adapt hybrid RY-mers to the existing concept of multi-context seeds and implement them in the read aligner strobealign. On simulated genomic and metagenomic datasets, we show that hybrid RY-mers result in higher mapping accuracy, while also reducing runtime by 4-6 times compared to the state-of-the-art aDNA alignment method BWA-aln. Furthermore, substituting aDNA aligner MALT in the metagenomic tool-suite aMeta with our new alignment approach demonstrated that aMeta gave a faster and less memory consuming detection of ancient taxa present in the samples.

title: Implicit Hierarchical Tensor Decomposition of Single-Cell Four-Omics Data Reveals Cell-Type-Linked Candidate Enhancer--Promoter-Associated Programs
abstract: Single-cell multi-omics provides complementary views of gene regulation, but integrating modalities with natural features comprising enhancers, genes, and three-dimensional (3D) genomic loci remains challenging. This study developed an implicit hierarchical tensor decomposition framework and applied it to the CHARM single-cell four-omics mouse brain data (GSE303006) by jointly analyzing ATAC, H3K27ac, RNA, and reconstructed 3D enhancer--promoter (E--P) distances. After quality control, 730,969 E--P pairs, 42,669 enhancers, 16,239 genes, 391,435 20-kb bin pairs, and 4,258 cells were retained. Each modality was independently reduced to 20 components and mapped to an implicit 730,969x4{,}258x20x4 tensor, which was decomposed without materializing the full array. In a joint model, cell type explained more variance than biological replicate for all 12 distinct cell components represented among the 100 largest Tucker core elements. A representative core linked the Inh_Ndnf/Lamp5--Ex_L3/4_IT cell axis to contrasting presynaptic-transmission and developmental/morphogenetic candidate E--P-associated programs. Its E--P and cell factors were recovered when the whole analysis was repeated independently on each pair of replicates, and the E--P pairs it prioritized agreed in direction with the cell-type-resolved enhancer--gene links of the original CHARM study. No single modality reproduced the program, which required the combination of accessibility, chromatin contact, and expression. Backprojection showed reproducible ATAC, H3K27ac, and 3D effects across three biological replicates; RNA differed clearly for the developmental module but not for the presynaptic module. The framework thus identifies regulatory structure that is shared across molecular modalities and is not recoverable from any single modality.

title: Simple models outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data exhibit strong and reproducible statistical structure. This has motivated the development of large-scale foundation models, such as TranscriptFormer, that use transformer-based architectures to learn a generative model for gene expression by embedding genes into a latent vector space. These embeddings have been used to obtain state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on downstream tasks such as cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Here, we ask whether similar performance can be achieved without utilizing computationally intensive deep learning-based representations. Using simple, interpretable pipelines that rely on careful normalization and linear methods, we obtain SOTA or near SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks commonly used to evaluate single-cell foundation models, including outperforming foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks involving novel cell types and organisms absent from the training data. Our findings highlight the need for rigorous benchmarking and suggest that the biology of cell identity can be captured by simple linear representations of single cell gene expression data.

title: Shared experimental materials inflate and reorder cross-participant decoding benchmarks
authors: Cui, H.; Zhu, Y.; Huang, S.; Xu, T.
abstract: Decoding mental states from brain activity underpins brain-computer interfaces and cognitive neuroscience. Decoders are judged by how well they generalize to people left out of training, taken as evidence that they capture what transfers between brains. However, most benchmarks present the same experimental materials to every participant, so held-out participants are tested on materials the model has already seen. Here we show, across 15 EEG, fMRI and eye-tracking datasets and 318 matched comparisons, that shared materials inflate cross-participant accuracy by up to 46 percentage points. They also reorder methods, reversing the advantage of foundation models over handcrafted features on the largest emotion EEG benchmark. The inflation tracks cross-participant item identifiability and, in sealed prospective tests, vanished where items could not be identified. Adding training items improved new-material accuracy more reliably than adding participants. These findings call for reporting new-material accuracy alongside conventional scores and for measuring item identifiability first.

title: Widespread oscillatory suppression in autism persists in the absence of psychotropic medication.
authors: Amorim, A. K. J.; Alves, G. M.; Pontes, G. C. L.; Dias, L.; Hondermann, B. M. F.; Silva, M. C. C.; Costa, L.; Ceriatte, C.; Pereira, A.; Brasil, L. M. B. F.; Souza, I. C. N.; Machado, C. L. M. V.; Lima, B.
abstract: Purpose: Investigate the neural oscillatory activity associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings in children and adolescents. Compare the corresponding oscillatory power between ASD patients taking psychotropic medication with a drug-naive group. Methods: ASD diagnosis was done using DSM-IV and CARS (Childhood Autism Rating Scale). EEG recordings employed 22 scalp electrodes (10/20 system). ASD vs. neurotypical groups were matched for sex and age (5 females; average age: ~10 years old). We analyzed the resting state (eyes open) EEG power spectrum during ~2-minute recordings. The multitaper FFT method was used to estimate spectral power for the delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma frequency bands. We pooled together data from several electrodes to compute comprehensive power spectra and assess the oscillatory behavior of macro brain regions. Results: We observed widespread (~4Hz - 20Hz) oscillatory suppression comprising the theta, alpha and beta frequency bands. The most widespread and robust ASD-associated power suppression was in the high theta and alpha bands. Delta and gamma bands showed no significant power change for any of the brain regions studied. Results from a subgroup of patients (N = 9) who never used psychotropics confirmed these findings, indicating that they are not an artifact of medication. Conclusion: Suppression in theta, alpha and beta oscillations may offer insights into the neurophysiological underpinnings of autism and could be used as an accessible and comprehensive tool in ASD diagnosis, regardless of the patients being or not on medication.

title: Accessing Mesoscale Functional Organization from Standard Functional MRI Leveraging AI-Based Super-Resolution
authors: Nasr, S.; Li, H. B.; Zemlyanker, D.; Huber, L.; Rosen, M. S.; Iglesias, J. E.
abstract: Access to the fine-scale functional organization of the human brain is essential for understanding cognition and neurological disorders yet remains beyond the reach of conventional functional MRI (fMRI) because of its limited spatial resolution and contrast-to-noise ratio. To overcome this limitation, we developed f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net-Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that enhances the effective spatial resolution of reconstructed fMRI magnitude images. The model was trained exclusively on high-resolution synthetic MRI data using extensive domain randomization and no adversarial or generative components. This approach enables robust out-of-the-box generalization (without retraining) to experimental datasets obtained with diverse acquisitions, while effectively curbing hallucination. Our experiments show that our publicly available model substantially improves the spatial fidelity of functional activation maps across multiple imaging paradigms and generalizes to a cohort of individuals with atypical brain function caused by amblyopia (lazy eye). F-LENNS consistently outperforms conventional resolution enhancement approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling and sharpening methods. These findings demonstrate that AI-driven super-resolution combined with domain randomization can overcome domain shifts arising from differences in MRI acquisition, enabling scalable, fine-scale functional brain mapping with widely available MRI hardware.

title: Rab10 and Arhgef7 interact to promote axon extension by linking vesicle supply and exocytosis
authors: Olocco, F.; Bekker, E.; Ravindran, P.; Pietralla, T.; Puschel, A. W.
abstract: The formation of functional neural circuits begins with the extension of a single axon by immature neurons. Axon elongation requires an expansion of the plasma membrane that depends on the polarization of vesicle trafficking and exocytosis. It is not completely understood how the increased transport of vesicles into the growing axon is linked to their subsequent insertion into the plasma membrane. An analysis of early stages of neuronal differentiation indicates that an asymmetry in neurite length precedes axon specification and the accumulation of PPVs in the nascent axon. We show that increasing the transport of vesicles in unpolarized neurons is sufficient to promote the extension of additional axons. This effect indicates that an increased supply of vesicles stimulates their subsequent insertion into the membrane to allow neurite growth. The link between vesicle transport and exocytosis is mediated by the interaction of Rab10 with Arhgef7. Rab10 stimulates Arhgef7 activity on PPVs as a GEF for Cdc42b to promote axon extension through exocyst-dependent exocytosis, suggesting that their interaction links the increased supply of PPVs to their exocytosis.

title: Geometric Kinematics of Human Eyes
abstract: In previous studies by the author on binocular vision with the asymmetric eye (AE), which models a healthy human eye with misaligned optical components, the results were primarily presented in the Rodrigues' vector (RV) framework and supported by simulations and 3D visualizations in GeoGebra's dynamic geometry environment. In this paper, the novel geometric kinematics of the human eye, that is, the eye with misaligned optics, and simplified assumptions about the eye rotations (the eye's translational movements are disregarded), are developed within the framework of rigid-body rotations. The originality of the analysis lies in a precise geometric decomposition of a full rotation of the eye's posture into a torsion-free rotation (the geodesic part) and a torsional rotation (the non-geodesic extension of the geodesic part). This decomposition is extended to the corresponding decomposition of the angular velocity. A novel derivation of the eye's angular velocity from the RV formulation of the eye kinematics is proposed.

title: SPOUT: An open-source hardware and software platform to study decision making while manipulating and recording from neural activity
authors: van den Boom, B. J. G.; Dash, D.; Rutherford, M.; Girasole, A. E.; Gorelik, P.; Mazor, O.; Sabatini, B. L.
abstract: Recording and manipulating brain activity during behavior is critical to understanding the underlying mechanisms of decision-making. Linking neural activity to behavior requires behavioral hardware and software tightly integrated with recording and perturbation systems on a shared clock. We built SPOUT (State-machine Platform for Operant Uni/dual-spout Tasks), an open-source, Teensy-driven state-machine platform with a MATLAB interface that runs 10 unique decision-making tasks (with dozens of variations available through user-friendly settings) to study behavior in head-restrained mice. The platform is built on several custom hardware devices: a dual-lick detector, headplate designs for optogenetics and two-photon calcium imaging, a three-axis motorized spout manipulator, and an optogenetics power modulator. The firmware differentiates between one and two lick spout tasks and can be controlled by a user-friendly interface. Task settings can be selected through the interface or by loading predefined settings files. We validated the clock speed and lick detection against an independent, external acquisition system and identified highly precise, sub-millisecond detection of single licks. Using a pseudo-random synchronization pulse generated by SPOUT, we corrected for missing data due to glitches in the acquisition system and clock drift. We showcase the versatility of SPOUT by training mice on an uninstructed lick-left/lick-right task in which the rewarded side switches unexpectedly and found that mice use history-dependent action-outcome associations to guide future behavior. Transiently inhibiting the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM) during cue presentation induced contralateral deficits, without affecting ipsilateral trials. Finally, two-photon imaging of ALM neurons revealed stronger population responses during contralateral choice licks compared to ipsilateral ones. Together, SPOUT offers an open-source, affordable platform to study decision-making in head-restrained mice while combining neural recordings and manipulations.

title: Sex differences in astrocytic reactivity and its association with cognitive decline in cognitively unimpaired older adults
authors: Reichert Plaska, C.; Jacobs, T.; Bruno, D.; Lee, S. H.; Imbimbo, B. P.; Osorio, R.; Benedet, A. L.; Ashton, N. J.; Zetterberg, H.; Pomara, N.; Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Astrocyte reactivity may contribute to increased Alzheimers disease (AD) risk in women. Although plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) levels have been reported to be higher in women than in men, few studies have examined sex-specific associations with other plasma AD biomarkers and cognition. METHODS: Participants were enrolled in the Memory Education and Research Initiative, a longitudinal community-based cohort, and underwent evaluation including blood biomarker sampling. The Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) was included as a replication cohort. RESULTS: Females had higher plasma GFAP levels than males in MERI (N{equiv}584), a finding that was replicated in ADNI. In MERI, higher baseline GFAP was associated with lower A{beta}42/40 and higher p-Tau231 and NfL levels. Higher baseline GFAP was also associated with steeper longitudinal decline in global cognition and episodic memory; however, GFAP x sex x time interactions were not significant. In ADNI, higher baseline GFAP was associated with higher p-Tau217 and NfL levels and with steeper longitudinal decline in global cognition and selected executive and semantic measures, without consistent evidence of sex-specific longitudinal effects. DISCUSSION: Plasma GFAP levels were consistently higher in females across two independent cohorts. GFAP was associated with AD-related blood biomarkers and longitudinal cognitive decline, but sex did not consistently modify these associations. These findings support a role for astrocytic reactivity in early AD-related processes while underscoring the need for further replication of sex-specific effects.

title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence
authors: Lokhandwala, S.; Cooper, R. E.; Hayes, R.; Sathe, S.; Elder, I.; Corcoran, M.; Horta, B.; Fray-Witzer, M.; Keller, L.; Chan, S.; Franzen, P.; Buysse, D.; Hasler, B. P.; Levenson, J. C.; Wallace, M. L.; Clark, D. B.; Blake, R. G.; Soehner, A.; Jalbrzikowski, M.
abstract: Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. We tested the ability of the Dreem3 sleep EEG headband to replicate established age effects in sleep physiology from late childhood through early adulthood. Typically developing youth (N=100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. We estimated age-related trends across eight macro-architecture and 15 micro-architecture variables with known age effects and conducted exploratory analyses of 24 additional variables. The Dreem3 replicated some established age trends, including increases in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 2%, and decreases in N3%, time in bed, NREM delta and theta power with increasing age. Although not all expected age-related associations reached statistical significance, like total sleep time and sleep efficiency, effect estimates were largely in the expected direction. These findings highlight the promise of wearable EEG devices for characterizing developmental sleep physiology while underscoring the need for further validation across sleep measures and age groups.

title: Nuclear retention and RNA editing safeguard self-tolerance to immunogenic intron lariats
authors: Lee, K.; Ku, J.; Park, S. Y.; Widowati, T. A.; Jeon, M.; Kim, N.; Chung, H.; Kim, M. J.; Kim, D. S.; Kim, H. Y.; Chung, H.; Jang, W. D.; Ryu, H. S.; Kim, Y.
abstract: Introns are excised as lariats and rapidly degraded upon linearization, leaving their post-splicing role unclear. Here, we investigate their immunoregulatory potential by analyzing the intron lariat landscape upon inhibition of the debranching enzyme DBR1. We find that lariats harboring transposable elements (TEs), especially inverted Alu repeats (IRAlus), elicit cell cycle-dependent activation of protein kinase R (PKR), but only in cells harboring a high burden, such as breast cancer. These immunogenic lariats are initially retained in the nucleus, but upon cytosolic release, they drive PKR activation and apoptosis. Exploiting this, we combine DBR1 depletion with anti-mitotic chemotherapy to enhance lariat-PKR interactions and promote cancer cell death in vitro and in vivo. We further show that A-to-I editing of IRAlus-containing lariats weakens their interaction with PKR and suppresses PKR activation. Our findings highlight two parallel molecular mechanisms to sustain self-tolerance to repeat-rich introns, revealing a vulnerability exploitable for anti-tumor therapy.

title: LOca-1: A minimal calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field
authors: Arsın, H.; Hribovsek, P.; Urich, L.; Fedoy, A.-E.; Stokke, R.; Mak, P.; Kaczorowska, A.-K.; ODonoghue, A. J.; Kaczorowski, T.; Steen, I. H.
abstract: Orthocaspases are prokaryotic homologs of metacaspases within the C14 family of cysteine proteases, yet their biochemical properties and cellular roles remain poorly understood. Here, we report the discovery and comprehensive characterization of LOca-1, a metagenome-derived orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field. LOca-1 consists primarily of a single, conserved p20 catalytic domain and undergoes calcium-dependent activation through cleavage at a conserved arginine residue. Once activated, LOca-1 displays strict arginyl-specific proteolytic activity and strong selectivity for residues surrounding the cleavage site. The enzyme is both thermoactive and thermostable, exhibiting maximal activity at 65 {degrees}C and a melting temperature of approximately 72 {degrees}C. Structural modelling revealed conservation of the catalytic core relative to plant metacaspases despite substantial sequence divergence. To our knowledge, LOca-1 is only the second biochemically characterized orthocaspase and the first reported from a deep-sea hydrothermal vent environment. LOca-1 expands the known biochemical diversity of prokaryotic metacaspase homologs and provides insights into the properties of a minimal p20-domain orthocaspase. Together, our findings establish LOca-1 as a thermostable, calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase and provide a foundation for future studies of orthocaspase function in prokaryotes.

title: A TMEM175 Mutation Disrupts the Lysosomal-Mitochondrial Axis Causing Short QT Syndrome and Sudden Cardiac Death
authors: Cruz, F. M.; Ruiz-Robles, J. M.; Martinez-Carrascoso, I. m.; Macias, A.; Moreno-Manuel, A. I.; Sanchez-Perez, P.; Corver, M.; Socuellamos, P. G.; Talavera-Gutierrez, A.; Bermudez-Jimenez, F. J.; Cabrera Borrego, E.; Macias-Ruiz, R.; Martinez, F.; Ochoa, J. P.; Jurgens, S. J.; Bezzina, C. R.; Jimenez-Jaimez, J.; Jalife, J.
abstract: Short QT Syndrome (SQTS) is a rare cardiac channelopathy characterized by abnormally short QTc intervals and increased sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk. Only 20-30% of SQTS cases have been linked to genetic mutations, typi-cally in surface membrane ion channels. We identified a novel lysosomal TMEM175 gene mutation (p.Arg377His) in 7 patients in a family with SQTS and SCD. Genetic analyses, including whole exome sequencing in the family and rare-variant burden testing in [~]118,000 UK Biobank participants, sug-gested an association between TMEM175 rare variants and QT interval short-ening. Functional studies in CRISPR-engineered mice and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) revealed that TMEM175R377H causes shortened QT intervals and hastened repolariza-tion, respectively, as well an increased arrhythmia susceptibility. Isolated TMEM175R377H cardiomyocytes showed action potential duration (APD) abbre-viation, confirmed in whole TMEM175R377H mouse hearts and patient-specific iPSC-CM monolayers. In silico and electron microscopy studies showed that TMEM175R377H disrupts lysosomal-mitochondrial interactions, leading to mito-chondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by the reduced maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity, with reduced ATP production, IKATP activation, and APD shortening. This mutation represents the first non-sarcolemmal ion chan-nel defect associated with SQTS and high SCD risk, potentially expanding the genetic landscape of the disease.

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis-primed neutrophils reshape the brain microenvironment to promote brain metastasis
authors: Endo, S.; Rujchanarong, D.; Keeran, K.; Jeffries, K.; Zhang, W.; Bannister, M.; Saeki, K.; Wei, D.; Tran, A.; Ellison, K.; Lee Fong, A.; Lim, L.; Kruhlak, M.; Lake, R.; Combs, C. A.; Steeg, P.; Kelly, M.; Lipkowitz, S.; Kanthi, Y.; Fujii, T.
abstract: Brain metastasis (BrM) is a devastating complication of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet how host macroenvironmental conditions influence brain metastatic susceptibility remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the impact of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), a common complication in patients with cancer, on TNBC brain metastasis. Analysis of a large clinical cohort identified DVT as an independent risk factor for BrM in patients with metastatic breast cancer. Using two syngeneic TNBC models, we demonstrated that DVT selectively enhanced brain metastasis without significantly affecting primary tumor growth or lung metastasis. Mechanistically, DVT increased neutrophil accumulation in the brain metastatic microenvironment, and neutrophil depletion completely abrogated the metastasis-promoting effect of DVT. Single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ cells in peripheral blood revealed that DVT reprogrammed circulating neutrophils toward migratory and inflammatory transcriptomic profiles characterized by neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. DVT increased CXCR2 expression on circulating neutrophils and enhanced neutrophil recruitment in brain. Moreover, DVT significantly increased circulating NETs. Collectively, our findings identify DVT as a systemic driver of TNBC brain metastasis and reveal that DVT primes circulating neutrophils toward enhanced vascular recruitment and NET formation, providing a mechanistic link between cancer-associated thrombosis and brain metastatic susceptibility.

title: A LOV-domain photoreceptor mediates phototaxis in brown algae
abstract: Phototaxis enables motile cells to navigate light environments and plays a critical role in survival and reproduction across diverse eukaryotic lineages. This ability has evolved independently through distinct photoreceptor systems. Yet, the molecular mechanisms underlying phototaxis remain poorly understood in many major eukaryotic lineages, including stramenopiles. Here, combining functional genetics, cell biology and evolutionary analyses, we identify Helmchrome (HELM), a LOV-domain protein required for phototaxis in the brown alga Ectocarpus. HELM localizes to the posterior flagellum and is responsible for the characteristic flavin-associated fluorescence of brown algal gametes. Loss of HELM abolishes phototactic accumulation and directional orientation without affecting basal motility or fertilization, demonstrating its specific requirement for light-directed movement. Phylogenetic analyses reveal that HELM-like proteins are distributed across diverse stramenopile lineages and that their domain architecture evolved through repeated duplication of an ancestral RGS-LOV module. Our findings identify HELM as a key component of the light-sensing machinery in brown algae, provide a molecular explanation for the long-standing observation of flagellar flavin fluorescence, and reveal a distinct phototaxis system that expands the known diversity of eukaryotic light-sensing mechanisms.
